transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-29
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (FlowGrok - Platform), Samir Khan (FlowGrok - SRE), Priya Das (FlowGrok - ML)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, short):
- Reviewed last week's throughput runs; noticed tail latency spikes at ~p95 when concurrency >12.
- SE proposed continuous-batching profile v2 with adaptive windowing; agreed to run extended 12h test.
- Action items: run longer run, share CSVs, confirm VPC egress, send pricing & SOW updates, schedule KV cache deep-dive.

Topics:
- Throughput numbers and stability, batching windows, concurrency targets, queue shaping, KV cache hit-rate, fallback strategy, pilot economics.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Alright, good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining, uh, quick roll call and then we'll jump into the throughput numbers.
[00:06] Lena Ortiz: Hi Maya, Lena here.
[00:08] Samir Khan: Samir on my side.
[00:10] Priya Das: Priya, hey all.
[00:12] Arjun Patel: Arjun from Redwood. Thanks for carving out time.
[00:15] Maya Chen: Cool. Quick agenda — recap last run, look at p95 and p99 spikes, talk continuous batching tune, concurrency targets, then next steps. Anything else to add?
[00:25] Samir Khan: Maybe the network egress question; we saw bigger egress numbers than expected so want to cover that.
[00:29] Maya Chen: Yep will cover.

[00:35] Arjun Patel: Okay so quick recap — last week we ran the 6h steady-state with mixed traffic profile you sent, priya, thanks for that. We saw average token throughput ~3.4k tokens/s across the pool, but when concurrency increased beyond 12 requests in flight we saw p95 latency jump from 180ms to ~620ms for that model at 2048 context. The cause tracing indicates batching windows were overshooting due to burst arrival patterns and KV cache miss amplification.
[01:05] Priya Das: Mm-hmm. We suspected the cache misses. Our model shards sometimes evict older KV entries — we have a shorter effective prefix reuse in weekends.
[01:13] Speaker 1: there's also the queueing backlog when the runtime tries to maintain throughput with fewer big batches, so latency suffers.
[01:18] Arjun Patel: Right. So proposal — two parallel changes: one, try continuous-batching profile v2 (smaller max batch, adaptive windowing with inter-request jitter smoothing) which limits the overshoot; and two, set soft concurrency target at 10 and allow burst to 16 with backpressure shaping. That combination reduced p95 spikes in our internal sim by about 40%.
[01:40] Samir Khan: For the sim numbers, can you share the sim config? We need to replicate locally.
[01:44] Arjun Patel: Yeah, I'll push the sim config and a CSV of the synthetic trace. It's the same arrival pattern you sent but with exponential bursts applied — I'll include exact param keys.
[01:52] Lena Ortiz: Also network — our egress was higher because responses included full tokens plus metadata. Are there ways to trim?
[01:58] Maya Chen: Two levers: structured output to reduce token generation (function calling), plus response compression and chunked streaming thresholds. We can also drop debug logs from payloads, and for pilot we can enable token-level sampling to limit max output length.
[02:14] Priya Das: On the KV side, we have a hypothesis the client side is re-sending full history on retries which kills cache hits.
[02:21] Speaker 2: mm-hmm.
[02:23] Arjun Patel: If that's true, we should instrument retries to preserve cached keys — add sticky session or keep-alive to maintain same server-side cache. For the pilot we recommend toggling prefix caching aggressively and increasing KV capacity for the runtime to test hit-rate impact.
[02:37] Samir Khan: Increasing KV capacity means more RAM on the worker nodes, right? What's the cost impact?
[02:42] Arjun Patel: Correct, more KV means a modest increase in memory footprint per GPU. Rough rule: 10% more KV -> ~6% more instance mem; cost increase depends on reserved capacity. For hosted pilot the delta is small; for dedicated you'd size your GPU types accordingly.
[02:55] Lena Ortiz: Can you give a ballpark of cost per million tokens with the new profile? We need to show finance.
[03:01] Maya Chen: We'll send updated numbers in the pricing doc but rough pilot estimate: with continuous batching + caching we see unit cost down ~18% compared to baseline. I'll send a spreadsheet.

[03:12] Arjun Patel: Back to tuning — one more change: adaptive queue shaping. Rather than fixed queue depth, tune the inflight queue buckets by percentile windows, so the system temporarily reduces batch size for tail-heavy windows. That keeps latency stable without sacrificing average throughput.
[03:30] Priya Das: This sounds good. Any risk of throughput collapse?
[03:33] Arjun Patel: There's a trade: if you shrink too aggressively you'll lower tokens/s. The soft concurrency target of 10 is the knob — it keeps the runtime in efficient batching regime. We can run sweep with targets 8,10,12 and measure tokens/sec vs p95.
[03:46] Speaker 1: For the sweep, we should capture GPU util, queue depth, kv_hit_rate, and request size distribution.
[03:51] Arjun Patel: Agreed. We'll produce CSVs with those metrics every minute.

[03:57] Samir Khan: About fallbacks — Priya asked earlier about model variants. If we fall back to a smaller quantized model during bursts will output quality degrade?
[04:05] Priya Das: For us, some tasks are sensitive. We need a way to route lower-risk requests to the smaller model but keep high-fidelity responses pinned.
[04:12] Maya Chen: Redwood can tag requests by route or request metadata. We can add routing policies so critical routes always go to the full model, others can go to the quantized variant. We'll include an example policy in the docs.
[04:23] Lena Ortiz: Good. Also do you support VPC private deployment? Our security team wants a private control plane, at least for dataset traces.
[04:31] Maya Chen: Yes, Private option available — we can do VPC peering and private control plane. For pilot we usually do hosted with private networking if they want faster setup; full private OOB takes longer.
[04:40] Samir Khan: Network egress numbers — I'll drop our sample swimlane trace in the shared folder.

[04:46] Arjun Patel: Cool. Now show of numbers from our quick local rerun (these are internal sim numbers): baseline steady-state 6h: avg tokens/s 3.4k, p95 180ms (low conc), p95 620ms (conc>12). With continuous-batching v2 + soft conc 10: avg tokens/s 3.1k, p95 220ms, p99 480ms. So small hit to average but big improvement on tail.
[05:12] Priya Das: So tokens/s dropped ~9% but p95 improved ~65% from the spike, that's acceptable.
[05:18] Arjun Patel: Yep. In production we'd iterate to recover some throughput by tuning batch size cap and inter-arrival smoothing.

[05:25] Speaker 3: question: how long should we run the test?
[05:28] Maya Chen: For signal on tail behavior we recommend 12 hours to capture diurnal variance and burst patterns; 24h if you have irregular bursts. For the pilot let's start with 12h.
[05:38] Samir Khan: Does Redwood provide tooling to replay a traffic trace?
[05:41] Arjun Patel: Yes we have a replay harness that can run your trace against different profiles and capture the metrics we discussed. I'll share the harness and instructions.

[05:48] Priya Das: For the replays, please include the metadata for seed, jitter, and whether retries are enabled. Our retries were a big factor.
[05:55] Arjun Patel: Will do.

[06:00] Maya Chen: Okay, let's summarize next steps — Arjun you'll run the 12h extended run with continuous-batching v2 and soft conc 10/16 burst; share CSV and sim config. Maya will update pilot pricing and include an optional dedicated sizing note and burst policy. Lena will provide the 7-day traffic trace and network egress numbers. Schedule KV cache deep-dive for next Wed. Any objections?
[06:24] Lena Ortiz: No objections, sounds good.
[06:26] Samir Khan: Good.

[06:28] Maya Chen: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in the shared drive and on the ticket.
